qa_pairs.question: What does Jess's first message reveal about her typical relationship to group travel commitments, and what about how she frames the Edinburgh experience suggests this outcome was not what she expected?
qa_pairs.answer: Jess opens Session 1 by noting she 'cannot believe' she almost cancelled the Edinburgh trip, then validates it: 'the flat was great, the group size felt right.' The fact that her primary feeling is relief at having attended — and that her opening word is about almost not going — reveals her habitual stance: she defaults to hesitancy on group travel and usually talks herself into cancelling near the deadline. The trip going well registers as a pleasant surprise rather than an expected outcome. The emphasis on what almost didn't happen, rather than what did, is the tell.

evidence_anchors.message_excerpt: I cannot believe I almost cancelled on that trip. the flat was great, the group size felt right
evidence_anchors.relevance: Jess's framing of the trip as something she nearly cancelled reveals her pre-existing pattern of last-minute hesitancy around group travel

qa_pairs.question: What pattern does Marcus's way of responding to group evening plans reveal about his relationship to the group's social schedule, and what is notable about how he communicates his absences?
qa_pairs.answer: Marcus consistently declines group evening plans with minimal explanation — brief, closed responses like 'Can't make tonight. Enjoy.' (Session 2) and 'I'll be out of town that weekend. Enjoy.' (Session 3). The notable quality is what he doesn't say: no excuse, no alternative offer, no elaboration. For a group where others share context freely, this brevity is itself communicative — it draws a boundary without explicitly naming one. Jess even notices the pattern in Session 3, joking that Marcus is 'always out of town for these things.' Marcus's response ('Just a lot of travel at the moment') maintains the same closed register, offering just enough to acknowledge the observation without opening a discussion.

evidence_anchors.message_excerpt: Can't make tonight. Enjoy.
evidence_anchors.relevance: Marcus declines with no explanation — a one-line response that reveals his consistent minimal-disclosure pattern

evidence_anchors.message_excerpt: I'll be out of town that weekend. Enjoy.
evidence_anchors.relevance: Second instance of the same pattern — different session, identical communicative style, confirming it as habitual rather than situational

qa_pairs.question: In the conversations, what does Zoe's way of responding when asked about her own plans or wellbeing suggest about how she relates to the group?
qa_pairs.answer: Across Sessions 1-3, whenever Zoe is directly asked about her plans or wellbeing, she deflects with a quip grounded in her work context rather than a direct answer. In Session 2, she declines the pub night with 'I'm on nights this week, can't make it.' In Session 3, when the group discusses whether she can make Joel's birthday, she responds: 'I say it every time because it's true every time. the NHS is not aware that Joel has a birthday.' The joke acknowledges the question while refusing to engage with it personally. Rory even names the pattern ('Zoe you say this every time'), suggesting it has become a recognisable feature of her communication. The shift format is consistent: work obligation → deflection → implicit availability unknown.

evidence_anchors.message_excerpt: I say it every time because it's true every time. the NHS is not aware that Joel has a birthday
evidence_anchors.relevance: Zoe deflects a direct question about availability with a hospital-based quip — acknowledges the question without answering it personally

evidence_anchors.message_excerpt: I'm on nights this week, can't make it. have a pint for me
evidence_anchors.relevance: Earlier instance of the same pattern — shift cited as the barrier, no personal context offered

qa_pairs.question: What in Rory's behavior on the walk suggested something had changed for him, and what does his explanation of that change tell us about what he was actually dealing with?
qa_pairs.answer: In Session 5, Aisha notices Rory is keeping pace on the walk's second half when he would usually fake stopping for a photo — a behavioral shift visible to the group. When asked, Rory says he's 'been taking the walks a bit more seriously recently — no particular reason,' then immediately deflects to asking for more chips. The phrase 'no particular reason' is a tell: when someone offers a reason and then negates it, they are usually signalling there is a reason they don't want to name. Zoe, with clinical training, catches this immediately ('no particular reason he says — noted Rory'), and Kezia confirms the behavioral shift is measurable ('your pace today was measurably different from the previous two walks'). The combination of visible physical change, deliberate understatement, and two group members flagging the evasion all point toward something Rory is managing privately — consistent with a health concern he has chosen not to disclose.

evidence_anchors.message_excerpt: I've been taking the walks a bit more seriously recently 🎒 no particular reason
